overview: Taíno describes diverse late precolonial Caribbean societies, especially in the Greater Antilles, rather than every population that previously lived on the islands. Their communities combined farming, ceremonial gatherings and connections maintained through travel across the sea.

periods.title: Chiefdoms and island connections
periods.summary: Chiefdoms organised ceremonial spaces and social relationships. Canoe travel connected communities, while local traditions varied across the islands.

periods.title: Conquest and profound disruption
periods.summary: European invasion brought forced labour, disease and attacks on Native authority. Survivors maintained knowledge and formed new relationships amid catastrophic loss.

periods.title: Living heritage documented
periods.summary: Museum records document family gardens, weaving and cultural renewal. These modern examples show continuing Native heritage and changing practices.

items.text: Starch analysis of clay griddles reveals different foods at neighbouring sites. El Flaco in the Dominican Republic yielded evidence especially of maize; La Luperona of zamia; and Palmetto Junction in the Turks and Caicos Islands of manioc. These are findings from sampled tools, not complete menus.

A clay griddle’s shape does not prove that it cooked only cassava bread. Microscopic residues reveal a wider range of plant preparation. Some surfaces may also have served for processing without heating, so researchers compare plant traces, damage and archaeological context.

The Smithsonian describes bohío houses made with local materials such as palms and vines. Its conuco examples show family gardens as working spaces whose crops changed after plants arrived from other continents.
Dried calabash gourds became bowls, spoons, containers and maracas. One plant supplied household utensils and musical instruments, joining practical work with performance.

Ceremonial plazas hosted batey, a team game played with a rubber ball. These substantial communal spaces also supported ritual gatherings. Their central position shows that organised recreation and public life mattered alongside subsistence work.

Areytos brought together storytelling, song, dance and drumming. Their forms varied with occasions such as celebrations, deaths or conflict. They carried collective knowledge through performance rather than following one uniform programme on every island.

A British Museum duho, or ritual seat, was carved from dense guayacan wood as a crouching human figure. Geometric patterns mark its back. The object combines furniture, bodily imagery and close attention to a difficult, durable material.

Gold inlays accent the duho’s eyes, mouth and shoulders. The museum interprets these features through chiefs’ and ritual specialists’ relationships with ancestor spirits. Its radiocarbon range, 1292 to 1399, concerns the wood; it cannot identify an exact day or year of carving.

sections.title: Seafaring and the journeys of objects

items.text: Canoes carried people and goods between islands. Colonial accounts describe arrivals from other islands for exchange, while decorated vessels could also express status. Maritime knowledge made water a route of social connection as well as a demanding physical environment.

Another duho, from Eleuthera in the Bahamas, has an inscription recording that James Thompson found it while enslaved around 1820. He was free when he sold it to a missionary in 1835. Its later collection history adds another colonial story to the older object.

The Smithsonian guide pictures Leonarda “Doña Esmeralda” Morales-Acevedo stripping maguey fibre for hammock thread in Puerto Rico. This named maker’s work documents living craft knowledge, while contemporary Taíno cultural movements challenge accounts that declare all Caribbean Native people extinct.

ending.text: Spanish colonization killed, displaced and enslaved Native people and undermined their political and religious institutions. Survivors carried knowledge into changing Caribbean communities. Contemporary Taíno identities and cultural renewal make an extinction ending inaccurate, even while the scale of colonial destruction must remain clear.
